chunks: Hamza ibn Muhammad ibn Ahmad ibn Ja'far ibn Muhammad ibn Zayd ibn Ali ibn al-Husayn ibn Ali ibn Abi Talib (peace be upon them) narrated to us. He said: Ali ibn Ibrahim ibn Hashim informed me in the year 307 AH. He said: My father narrated to us. He said: Muhammad ibn Abi 'Umayr narrated to us, from Hafs ibn al-Bakhtari, from al-Sadiq Ja'far ibn Muhammad, from his father, from his grandfather (peace be upon them), who said:

A quarrel and dispute occurred between Salman al-Farisi (may God have mercy on him) and a man. The man said to him: Who are you, Salman? So Salman said: As for my beginning and your beginning, it was an impure drop of sperm. As for my end and your end, it will be a rotting corpse. On the Day of Resurrection, when the scales are placed, the one whose scale is heavy is the noble one, and the one whose scale is light is the vile one.

key_terms.الكريم: Al-Karim - The noble/generous one; here referring to one whose good deeds outweigh the bad
key_terms.اللئيم: Al-La'im - The vile/base one; here referring to one whose bad deeds outweigh the good
key_terms.الموازين: Al-Mawazin - The Scales of the Day of Judgment on which deeds will be weighed
key_terms.جيفة: Jifa - A corpse/carcass, referring to the inevitable decomposition after death
key_terms.نطفة: Nutfa - A drop of sperm/seminal fluid, referring to the humble biological origin of every human being

ai.seo_question: What did Salman al-Farisi say about human equality and the true measure of nobility in Islam?
ai.summary: Salman al-Farisi, the renowned Persian companion of the Prophet, was challenged about his identity by a man who sought to demean him. Salman's response elegantly demolished racial and social pride by pointing out the shared biological origin and fate of all humans. In the early Islamic community, where tribal lineage was paramount, Salman's words carried revolutionary weight: true nobility comes only from one's deeds as weighed on the Day of Judgment, not from birth or ethnicity.
word_analysis: may He have mercy on him
